name: PG&E
rate_note: Averaged across Tier 1 and Tier 2 Time-of-Use (E-TOU-C) rates; peaks can exceed $0.50/kWh in summer. Excludes fixed delivery charges.

export_compensation.summary: PG&E operates under the Solar Billing Plan (NEM 3.0). Homeowners do not receive a 1:1 retail credit for solar exported to the grid. Instead, exported power is credited at an avoided cost rate, which averages $0.05 - $0.08/kWh during midday. To achieve a return on investment, homeowners must install a home battery to store excess solar during the day and discharge it during peak evening hours.

interconnection.typical_size_notes: Residential systems are typically under 30 kW. Systems exceeding 30 kW face significantly higher review scrutiny and potential transformer upgrade costs.
interconnection.pto_notes: Permission to Operate (PTO) takes an average of 15 to 45 days after the municipal electrical inspection is passed.

steps.title: Interconnection Application (Pre-Install)
steps.body: Your installer submits a site plan, single-line electrical diagram, and equipment specifications (verifying active UL 1741 and IEEE 1547 compliance) to the PG&E portal before physical installation begins. PG&E runs a hosting capacity screen to ensure the local transformer can handle the load.

steps.title: Local AHJ Permitting & Construction
steps.body: Once PG&E approves the engineering review, the local city or county building department issues a permit. The physical solar and battery installation occurs, usually taking 1 to 3 days.

steps.title: Municipal Electrical Inspection
steps.body: A local building inspector visits your home to verify the system meets NEC Article 690 codes and rapid-shutdown safety requirements. Passing this inspection is required before the utility will grant PTO.

steps.title: Permission to Operate (PTO)
steps.body: Your installer forwards the signed municipal job card to PG&E. PG&E reviews the documentation, reprograms your smart meter for bidirectional data, and issues an official PTO letter. Only then can you legally energize the system.

local_permitting_notes: California's SolarAPP+ streamlines the local AHJ permit step for PG&E customers in participating municipalities, reducing initial permit approval times. Under the California Solar Rights Act, HOAs cannot legally ban solar installations, though they can dictate reasonable aesthetic placement.
headline: Is solar worth it with PG&E in 2026?
summary: Homeowners who installed solar with PG&E years ago brag about 1:1 net metering, but today's shoppers face the Solar Billing Plan (NEM 3.0). Because PG&E pays pennies for exported power — and the federal 25D credit no longer applies to 2026 cash/loan installs — solar math usually requires a battery for self-consumption and peak avoidance.

sections.heading: Why PG&E bills trigger solar research
sections.body: PG&E possesses some of the highest and most volatile electricity rates in the United States, with average residential rates hovering near $0.38/kWh and peak summer rates frequently crossing $0.50/kWh. Homeowners usually seek out solar after unexpected seasonal bill spikes. With the expiration of the 30% federal tax credit for cash purchases in 2026, the economics rely entirely on avoiding PG&E's retail rates through self-consumption. Sizing a system simply to match 100% of usage with panels alone no longer works; systems must be sized alongside a battery to load-shift away from the 4 PM to 9 PM time-of-use window.

sections.heading: SGIP Battery Rebates in 2026
sections.body: PG&E customers may be eligible for the state-mandated Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP). While general market funds are largely exhausted, the 2026 program prioritizes low-income households, Medical Baseline customers, and homes in Tier 2/3 High Fire-Threat Districts that experience Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS). Eligible Equity Resiliency customers can receive substantial per-kWh battery incentives — confirm current funding before signing.

sections.heading: What happens after you say yes
sections.body: Local building permits and PG&E Rule 21 interconnection are separate gates. Passing a city electrical inspection does not grant Permission to Operate. Expect PTO roughly 15–45 days after inspection paperwork reaches PG&E.

faqs.question: Can I still get NEM 2.0 with PG&E?
faqs.answer: No. The deadline to be grandfathered into NEM 2.0 passed in April 2023. All new solar applications submitted to PG&E fall under the current Solar Billing Plan (NEM 3.0).

faqs.question: Does the 30% federal solar tax credit still apply?
faqs.answer: For homeowner-owned systems placed in service after December 31, 2025, Section 25D is generally unavailable. Confirm with a tax advisor. Some lease/PPA structures may still reflect commercial credits.
